hints.junior: The new semantic search felt smarter but slower — every keystroke round-tripped to a server for a docs set of maybe 40 pages that rarely changed.
hints.mid: 400-700ms per query, paid on a corpus small and static enough that a one-time client-side load would have made queries after the first essentially free.
hints.staff: The mistake was defaulting to server-side without checking whether this corpus's size and change frequency actually justified a round trip per keystroke.

hints.junior: Type a search term in each mode — one waits on a network call every time, the other loads once and answers instantly after.
hints.mid: Broken mode simulates a real round trip per query. Fixed mode simulates one model load, then zero-network local search after.
hints.staff: The fixed mode's cost isn't gone, it moved earlier — compare the one-time load against the broken mode's cost repeating on every query.

hints.junior: Client-side downloads a model and the docs' vectors once, then searches locally. Server-side sends the query and waits for a round trip, every time.
hints.mid: Client-side pays a one-time cold start; server-side pays a per-query round trip — which wins depends on corpus size and search volume.
hints.staff: A third variable beyond size: change frequency. Client-side needs a re-shipped index on every content change; server-side re-indexes independently of any deploy.

hints.junior: This demo's corpus is eight documents on purpose — a client-side index at that size is nothing. Hundreds of pages changes the math.
hints.mid: No fixed page-count flips the answer — model size, searches per session, and whether the download can be prefetched all factor in.
hints.staff: A hybrid is legitimate: client-side index for the fixed core, server-side fallback for anything not yet baked into the shipped index.

sections.junior: Hey! This one's about a docs sidebar that got a smarter search feature and somehow got slower at the same time, because every single search had to round-trip to a server for a doc set that barely ever changed.
sections.mid: The round-trip latency was the visible symptom, but for a small, rarely-changing doc set shipped with the app, computing search entirely client-side would have made every query after the first effectively free.
sections.staff: The mistake wasn't choosing server-side search, it was choosing it by default without checking whether this corpus actually justified a network round trip on every keystroke.

sections.junior: There are really two ways to run this kind of search. Ship the model to the browser and search locally after one upfront download, or send every query to a server and wait for a response each time. Which one wins depends on how big your content is and how often it changes.
sections.mid: Client-side pays a one-time cold-start cost before the first search can run; server-side pays a per-query cost, a round trip, every time — a fixed small doc set favors client-side, a large or changing one favors server-side.
sections.staff: There's a third variable beyond size: how often the corpus changes. Client-side needs its index rebuilt and re-shipped on every content change — fine on a release cadence, painful for hourly updates.

sections.junior: Try searching the same small set of documents both ways. One mode makes a real network call on every search. The other loads once, up front, and then every search after that is instant.
sections.mid: Broken mode simulates a real round trip on every query. Fixed mode simulates a one-time model download, then every search after that has no network call at all.
sections.staff: The fixed mode's cost isn't gone, it's moved earlier — watch the one-time load happen before the first query, then compare per-query latency after that.

sections.junior: For a small set of content that doesn't change much, doing search fully in the browser after one upfront load usually wins. For a big or fast-changing set, sending the query to a server usually wins. Pick based on your actual content, not on which one sounds more advanced.
sections.mid: Client-side pays once and is free per query after; server-side pays nothing upfront but costs a round trip every time — match the choice to corpus size and change frequency.
sections.staff: The two approaches can coexist in the same feature rather than being all-or-nothing.
